text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London ended lower and it seems as if the market has run out of steam at the moment. Probably players have recognized that there is no shortage of robusta coffee in contrast to tight supplies in the arabicas sector.

The International Coffee Organization (ICO) recently said that spiralling coffee markets face a risk of big falls in prices if investment funds liquidate their massive positions built over the past few months. May lost $20 to close at $2,020 per tonne, while July gave up $25 to close at $2,075 per tonne.

Arabica futures in New York ended lower across the board on profit taking after the tremendous run-up in values over the past few weeks. July lost 6.00 cents/lb to close at 240.25 cents/lb, while September closed 5.30 cents/lb lower at 214.70 cents/lb.
Focus this week is likely to be in London, where the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) is meeting to discuss its policy on export quotas in view of the recent explosive futures rally.

It is not excluded that the group will lift all export restrictions. However, that would be largely cosmetic, as the question is to what extent countries adhered to the export restrictions anyhow. The outlook for the market remains bullish until at least mid-July when the risk of frost is greatly reduced and new Brazilian supplies are coming in.

COLOMBIA - The head of Colombia's National Coffee Growers Federation (FNC) said he expected the coming October/September 1997/98 crop to be a normal crop of 12.2 million bags, up from 10.2 million bags expected for 1996/97.

However, it is fairly early to make any firm predictions for next season's crop. Cardenas said a poor 1996/97 crop of 10.2 million bags is forcing a draw down in stocks to meet requirements. He said 1.2 million bags have already been withdrawn from the Federation's stocks since October.

He added, stocks at the end of April totalled 4.8 million bags, although he noted that not all of the coffee is of exportable quality and some stocks need to be held for domestic consumption. Cardenas said Colombia's annual commitments to export are 11.5 million bags while domestic consumption is steady at 1.6 million bags yielding a total of 13.10 million bags. With a crop of around 12 million bags forecast for 1997/98 there will be another shortfall and the country will have little stocks to draw from.

UGANDA - Coffee production in 1996/97 (October/September) may exceed 4.0 million 60-kgs given encouraging prospects for the mid-crop, official sources said. This is higher than the 3.8 million bags expected so far. 1995/96 production was around 4.2 million bags. An estimate for 1997/98 will not be available until July, official sources said.

SWITZERLAND - Switzerland imported 73,212 bags of coffee in February 1997, nearly 14 per cent less than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1997 up to 179,800 bags, nearly 10 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1996. Total imports in calendar year 1996 rose by 7 per cent to 1.121 million bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/February 1997 were Brazil (17,800 vs 18,900 bags) and Colombia (26,900 vs 41,500 bags). The country exported 48,500 bags of coffee in January/February 1997, 33 per cent more than was exported the same period in 1996. Total exports in calendar year 1996 rose by 33 per cent to 245,000 bags.

DENMARK - Denmark imported 87,100 bags of coffee in January 1997, 10 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. Total imports in calendar year 1996 rose by 15 per cent to 1.008 million bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January 1997 were Brazil (41,200 vs 23,900 bags) and Colombia (21,600 vs 20,800 bags).
